title: The Mocking Bird (poem)
text:
THE MOCKING BIRD

A fancied conversation between Professor R. R. Halsell and a mockingbird, a poem contributed from the pen of Guy F. Webb, in memory of the old school.

[The poem is set in two columns. It imagines a dialogue between Professor Halsell and a mockingbird recalling the old Savoy College days. Portions are difficult to read at this scan resolution.]

"In what subtle realm, sweet bird,
    Learned thou thy mocking song?
What pranking sprite within thee stirred,
    The neighbors thus to wrong?

"Was there no joy that ought
    For thee less fortunate?
No lesson, good, with kindess fraught,
    To me wouldst[?] thou relate?"

"All other birds, each has one song,
    Which fills his cup to brim,
'Tis thou, of all the merry throng,
    And soul his song from him.

"And, sat content to sing thine own,
    And have to each his gem,
In sweeter notes than they had known,
    Tho' sing their songs to them.

"Can it be true that in the realm
    Where music gave thee voice,
My ear[?] of weak, did overwhelm,
    O'er th' weak, the strong rejoice?

"Or wast thou sent, a master apt,
    To teach the feathered host;
And hadst thy songs from them fore-
    hapt[?],
    Nor one a song could boast?

"And are we wrong when we con-
    demn,
    And call thee, 'Mocking Bird'?
And dost thou teach their songs to
    them,
    Thy songs alone are heard?"

The bird replied: "I am surprised
    That you should so esteem;
And that a voice from out the skies
    Should mean no more to you.

"'Tis with us mocking mind I sing,
    A fashion making host;
I sing thee modestly[?].

"Then, sir, you see, 'tis not with me
    A foolish mocking brawl;
With grief or cheer, I am sincere,
    I sympathize with all."
notes: Poem 'The Mocking Bird' by Guy F. Webb imagining a conversation with Professor R. R. Halsell. Set in two columns; several lines uncertain at scan resolution and marked [?].
